children: By Emma Tucker
From My Desk

Profits are soaring at America's biggest companies — and their leaders say that likely won't change soon. From Target and J.M. Smucker to farm-equipment maker Deere, companies spanning the breadth of the U.S. economy are ringing up heftier sales and earnings. Many have raised financial outlooks for the year. Chalk the good times up to a confluence of fortunate events: red-hot AI spending, federal spending and the windfall companies are getting in the form of refunds of some of their past tariff payments. Plus, a booming stock market and high home values are helping many shoppers keep spending, even as plenty of others struggle to absorb rising prices. What are they buying? New appliances, toys and clothing.
Today's Headlines
U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers in the Strait of Hormuz, marking the first American strike in weeks and heightening the risk of a return to all-out conflict.
The death toll from the floods in Nepal and China surpassed 900, as army and police teams raced to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped inside mountain tunnels.

SB Energy issued OpenAI warrants worth an estimated $5.5 billion to land the AI company as a data-center tenant. The Softbank-backed company is expected to make its IPO filing public as soon as this week.
Japan plans to shift more of its military spending toward drones and missiles and build up supplies of ammunition, as officials eye a record defense budget for the next fiscal year.

Investors in the Opportunity Zone program — the first Trump administration's tax incentive to push capital into low-income areas — are approaching the crucial Dec. 31 date when they must include long-deferred capital gains in their taxable income.
To help Apple reach new heights, incoming CEO John Ternus must take it beyond the supply-chain mastery of Tim Cook and rev up its innovation engine, especially in AI.
Live From The Markets
Follow our live financial coverage all day.
For years, it paid off to buy stocks that were rising in price — and bet against struggling shares. Suddenly, the momentum trade is a loser.
Shein is making a bold choice, going ahead with its IPO when its growth is looking shabby. While the fast-fashion giant's shares aren't a bargain, they aren't castoffs either, writes Jinjoo Lee.
Read It Here First
A summer for the ages scorched French grapes, English gardens — and Europe's economy.

This was the hottest June-to-July period on record in Western Europe, according to Copernicus, the European Union's Earth observation program. Wildfires turbocharged by the heat and lack of rain decimated France and Spain. Rivers across central Europe nearly ran dry. Crops withered, riverboats ran aground, trains derailed. The pace of change has caught many European governments off guard, despite years of warnings from scientists, report David Luhnow, Stacy Meichtry and Ed Ballard. The shifting climate will transform business as usual for governments, companies, farmers and ordinary people.
A geopolitical mismatch is driving Russia to threaten the West.

Moscow faces a fundamental asymmetry as it seeks to beat Ukraine into submission, writes Yaroslav Trofimov. Kyiv can rely on a secure hinterland beyond its borders — its European neighbors — for economic resilience and military logistics. The Kremlin has no such backup. Hits to Russia's militarized economy translate more directly into damage to the country's ability to keep the war going. This lopsided geopolitical setup offsets, to a significant degree, Russia's advantage in firepower. It has also become the key reason driving what Western officials say is a widening Russian campaign of sabotage, hacking and other hybrid operations aimed at intimidating European leaders and voters.

See The Story
These young New Yorkers scored the ultimate deal: a rent-stabilized apartment.

Fewer Gen-Z and millennial renters have been able to break into the coveted housing stock, according to an analysis by the city comptroller. Baby-boomer and Gen-X renters are loath to give up their deals. And old rent-stabilized properties are getting torn down for development projects, shrinking the number available. The young rent-stabilized tenants of New York City represent a rare breed of their generation. A few of them opened their doors to show us their apartments.
Happening Today
President Trump is scheduled to make an announcement on healthcare affordability at 3 p.m. ET.
The House of Representatives returns from its August recess.
G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are meeting today and tomorrow in North Carolina.
Number Of The Day

The fee Capital One recently began charging its Venture X cardholders to bring a guest to one of its airport lounges, unless they spend at least $75,000 a year. The perk used to be free. Higher annual fees are forcing premium credit cardholders to work harder to get their money's worth — and tightened rules around rewards and perks aren't making it any easier.
And Finally. . .
This Olympic hockey player is a global expert on Caesar salads.

Aerin Frankel — the goaltender for the U.S. women's national ice hockey team — has eaten more of the dish than she can reliably count and formally reviewed dozens on Instagram. She's tried them everywhere from McDonald's to Michelin-starred haunts, in tony European hamlets and Midwestern hockey towns. Recent ratings include a shrimp Caesar in Palm Beach, Fla., (8.3 out of 10) and a bulky chicken Caesar wrap in Minnesota that earned a 9.5, one of Frankel's highest-ever scores.
